# SpeedProfiling Project (Baylor Football Velocity Profiling)

SpeedProfiling is a Baylor football velocity-profiling project that pulls full-game 10 Hz Catapult GPS data, aligns it with college football play-by-play (via CFBD / cfbfastR), and produces per-athlete speed/velocity profiles adapted from a workshop method authored by "Alex." The project is developed as a private R repository (`github.com/erash11/SpeedProfiling`, 176-package renv lockfile) executed against a 7-ticket implementation plan tracked in the KeystoneOS `.scratch/speedprofiling/issues/` directory, using the mattpocock `implement` and `code-review` skills. On 2026-07-18, tickets 01, 02, 04, and 07 were advanced; on 2026-07-20, ticket 05 (GPS↔play-by-play merge, on-field separation, workload tables) was closed and shipped on PR #3.

## Key Points

- **Ticket-driven, per-session workflow:** the project is decomposed into 7 tickets; each ticket is implemented in a fresh session via `/mattpocock-skills:implement <ticket path>`. The `Status:` line in each ticket file is the claim mechanism that prevents parallel-session collisions. Eric prefers fresh parallel sessions per ticket over driving all tickets from one session.
- **catapultR credentials-object API change:** the installed catapultR uses a new credentials-object API — `ofCloudCreateToken(sToken=…, sRegion='America')`; the old `token=` argument no longer exists. `R/01_get_data.R` was rewritten for this API in ticket 04.
- **Deleting a token file does not revoke it server-side:** the old 2023 Catapult token had to be revoked manually in the OpenField UI — removing the local JWT file does not invalidate the token on Catapult's servers. Ticket 02 hardened `.gitignore` against `AccessTokens.txt`/`*token*.txt` and migrated live values into `.Renviron`, but server-side revocation of a superseded token is a separate manual step (logged as an Eric-manual action item).
- **Full 10 Hz pull verified (ticket 04):** the pull retrieved 8,932,931 rows at true 10 Hz (0.1 s spacing, max velocity 20.3 mph) for all 61/61 athletes (79 MB, gitignored) plus 188 play-by-play plays; 69/69 testthat tests pass. A feasibility probe gate hard-stops before the bulk pull unless genuine 10 Hz rows with all required columns return.
- **Ticket 05 — GPS↔play-by-play alignment (2026-07-20):** merged 10 Hz GPS with play-by-play using the kickoff surge signature as a numerical time anchor, separated on-field from sideline athletes via a two-part rule (sideline boundary + metabolic-power gate), and produced per-play workload tables. Closed on PR #3. See [[concepts/speedprofiling-gps-playbyplay-alignment]].
- **Game selection is config, not code:** game selection moved from hardcoded `GAME_*` variables to a `GAMES` table in `R/config.R` (activity ID + cfbd args per row). Adding a game is a one-row config edit; an empty `GAMES` renders the activity list to pick from. Per-game `.rds` caching pays the slow pull once.
- **Stacked PRs merge in order #1 → #2 → #3;** ticket 04's PR #2 is stacked on ticket 03's PR #1.

## Details

The project adopts a set of workshop R scripts (from an author "Alex") as reference material and re-implements them ticket by ticket against Baylor's live data sources. Ticket 01 established the repo, adopted the Drive scripts/docs, and set FERPA rules in AGENTS.md with a CLAUDE.md adapter, gitignore protection, and a private repo. A standards review of the adopted scripts found four real defects — notably a timestamp-conversion bug in `01_get_data.R` and play-end windows in `02_combine_data.R` that erroneously absorb halftime gaps — which were logged to the tracker and mapped to downstream tickets 03–06 rather than patched twice in reference code. Ticket 02 decoded the Catapult JWT scopes (`connect, catapultr, sensor-read-only`, expiry 2126), confirming the sensor scope needed for the 10 Hz feasibility probe, and migrated tokens from an untracked `AccessTokens.txt` (hardened out via `.gitignore` patterns `AccessTokens.txt` and `*token*.txt`) into `C:\Users\eric_rash\Documents\.Renviron` (`CATAPULT_TOKEN`, `CFBD_API_KEY`). Two environment notes surfaced during setup: the local `G:\My Drive` mount is much faster for adopting workshop files than downloading them through the Drive API, and `reactablefmtr` was archived off CRAN so it must be installed from GitHub for a clean renv restore (the renv snapshot-type setting also had to be fixed for `renv::status()` to report clean).

Ticket 04 delivered the core game-data pull (8.9M rows at true 10 Hz for 61 athletes), verified end-to-end (69/69 tests, both `.rds` caches hit on re-run). The BYU game (BYU – G5 – 09.28.24) was auto-selected because ticket 02 had already verified its play-by-play and Eric was unavailable to pick interactively; swapping games is a one-row `GAMES` config edit. Ticket 04 anticipated two forward-looking findings for ticket 05: Catapult X/Y coordinates return in venue coordinates requiring a transform, and the cfbfastR `wallclock` column might simplify GPS↔play timestamp alignment. Ticket 05 (2026-07-20) resolved both — the venue-coordinate issue via PCA field-frame recovery and the timestamp alignment via the kickoff surge signature rather than `wallclock`. A recurring environment note: background R tasks can report a false "exit code 1" even when the script log shows a clean end-to-end run, so the log must be checked before assuming failure (see [[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]]). Ticket 03 (analysis core + tests) and ticket 07 (KeystoneOS/SecondBrain integration) were also run as parallel fresh sessions, and ticket 06 (velocity profiles — sprint detection, NLS fits, bootstrap CIs, position-group comparisons) remains downstream.

# A Router Pointing at a Wrong Answer: Stale DEV Memory After the Mac Migration

The sharpest finding of the 2026-09-02 memlint run was structural rather than factual. `project_dev-layout-and-discovery.md` still claimed the `DEV` directory lived at `~/Desktop/DEV` — a Windows-era layout — while `DEV/CLAUDE.md` explicitly routed all layout questions *to that file*. The wrong fact was therefore not merely present in memory; it was the designated authority on its own topic. Roughly eight DEV memory files carried similar Windows-era claims, and all of them loaded into every session.

## Key Points

- **Delegation multiplies the cost of a stale fact.** A wrong claim sitting in an unreferenced file is one bad data point; a wrong claim in a file that another document names as the canonical source is the answer to every question on that topic.
- **The stale claim survived the platform that produced it.** `~/Desktop/DEV` was correct on Windows and became wrong on macOS, with nothing in the migration path that would notice or flag the discrepancy.
- **Scale matters: ~8 DEV memory files carried Windows-era claims, and they loaded every session.** Unlike a stale file on disk that is read only when opened, memory-tier staleness is paid on every conversation.
- **Establishing a canonical pointer creates an obligation to verify the target.** `DEV/CLAUDE.md`'s routing line was itself correct and useful; the defect was that nothing re-checked the pointed-at content after the host changed.
- **This is what made stale memories the higher-priority cleanup** over the 23 broken `[[links]]`: a broken link fails loudly and resolves to nothing, while a stale router answers confidently and wrongly.

## Details

The failure has the same root as the other Windows-artifact survivals catalogued in [[connections/windows-defaults-outlive-the-windows-machine]]: a fact captured at one moment on one host, frozen into a durable artifact, and never re-verified when the host changed underneath it. What distinguishes this instance is the routing layer. Canonical-source pointers are a good pattern — they prevent the same fact from being restated in five places and drifting apart — but they concentrate risk, because the correctness of every consumer now depends on the correctness of one target. The relocation discipline in [[concepts/canonical-section-relocation-inbound-pointers]] deals with the same coupling from the other direction, where moving a canonical section leaves inbound pointers dangling; here the pointer resolves fine and delivers a wrong answer, which is strictly harder to detect.

Memory-tier staleness is also more expensive than ordinary file staleness because of when it is read. A stale README costs something only when someone opens it. A stale memory file that is injected at session start is consulted implicitly in every conversation, shaping paths, assumptions, and tool invocations without ever being displayed for review. Eight such files in the DEV slug means eight Windows-era premises silently in play at the start of every DEV session. That asymmetry is the concrete argument behind the session's option-A-over-option-B choice: broken `[[links]]` degrade retrieval, whereas stale facts degrade reasoning, and the latter fails silently.

The remedy implied by the finding is not a one-time correction but a verification obligation attached to the pointer itself. Wherever one document declares another the authority on a topic, the pair should be re-checked together whenever the underlying environment changes — a migration, a directory reorganization, a tool replacement. Absent that, the routing relationship converts a single stale file into a systematically wrong answer, and the confidence with which it is delivered is proportional to how well the routing was designed.

# Merging a Restored Claude Code Config Without Overwriting the Local Copy

On 2026-10-11 a full Windows Claude Code restore (48,765 files) was merged into the Mac's `~/.claude/` directory. The merge was done in two passes: a dry run that counted what would be new, then a real copy that added files without overwriting any existing Mac file. Where the two machines held different versions of the same file, the Mac copy was kept and the Windows copy was saved beside it with a `.from-windows` suffix.

## Key Points

- **Dry run first.** A dry run counted 16,814 new files; the real merge copied 16,751. The gap between the two numbers was itself a signal worth checking before the real run.
- **Mac wins in place; Windows is preserved as a sidecar.** 7,739 files differed between machines. Each Mac file stayed as is, and the Windows version was saved as `<file>.from-windows`, so nothing was lost and no decision was forced at merge time.
- **Some copied files did not persist.** 898 files from the merge were absent after the copy. They were mostly orphaned plugin cache under `plugins/cache/claude-video/`, old backup files, and a Windows link `skills/grill-with-ui`. The cause of the remaining discrepancy was not established.
- **Credentials came along in the merge.** `.credentials.json` and `CREDENTIALS.md` were copied into `~/.claude`. Whether to keep them there, move them out, or rotate the keys was left as an open decision.
- **Partial archives were kept.** Three partial zips were retained in `~/Restore/_zips/` at the user's choice.

## Details

A cross-machine restore is a two-writer merge with no shared history to resolve against. Git-tracked config can use three-way merge, but a raw restore of a home-directory tree has only two versions of each file and no common ancestor. The sidecar convention handles this by refusing to pick a winner. The Mac version keeps the live path, which matters because the Mac is the machine currently in use, and the Windows version is retained as evidence rather than discarded. The 7,739 `.from-windows` files are therefore a review queue, not a set of conflicts that must be resolved before continuing. The same convention appears in the sync tooling elsewhere in this knowledge base, where a `.from-*` suffix marks an unresolved cross-machine copy.

The dry-run-then-copy order is a cheap guard against an unexamined assumption. The dry run confirms that the merge will add files rather than replace them, and its count gives a baseline to compare against afterward. The 898-file shortfall shows why the baseline matters: the count did not reconcile, and the session recorded it as an open question rather than assuming the copy was complete. Newer copies are not automatically more complete, and a restore that reports success still needs its output checked against what was expected.

The credentials decision is the item with the highest consequence. Copying `.credentials.json` into a synced home directory widens the exposure of a secret that already lived on another machine. The session deferred the choice to the user and suggested two options: keep the file where it is, or move it out and rotate the keys. Rotation is the stronger option when a copy has traveled through a backup or sync path, consistent with the lesson in [[concepts/git-history-credential-exposure]] that a secret persisting in any copy requires revocation rather than cleanup alone.

## Related Concepts

- [[connections/newer-is-not-more-complete]] — Why a merge should add or deduplicate, and why a smaller newer copy is a warning sign.

- [[concepts/cross-machine-conflict-file-triage]] — Triage of cross-machine conflicts by artifact kind rather than a blanket rule.
- [[concepts/git-history-credential-exposure]] — Why a credential copied across machines requires rotation, not just removal.
- [[connections/windows-defaults-outlive-the-windows-machine]] — Windows-era settings and paths that a restore carries into the Mac environment.

# Milvus Lite Single-Writer Lock Held by an Orphaned Index Process

On macOS, memsearch uses Milvus Lite, a file-backed vector store that permits only one writer at a time. On 2026-10-11 hook failures were traced to a chain of index processes that each held the database lock. Process 14423, started at 19:41 by a sync-hook timeout streak, exited on its own by 22:41. Process 64563, a sync-hook worker started at 22:18, took the lock immediately and was still running at 22:57. The debugging established that a lock file alone does not prevent this chain, and that an orphaned process cannot be cleaned up by the job that spawned it.

## Key Points

- **Lock contention is a single-writer constraint, not a bug in the indexer.** Windows runs Milvus in Docker as a multi-client server, so concurrent writers are normal there. The Mac's Milvus Lite is a single-writer file, so any second writer waits or fails.
- **Lock handoff can cascade.** When one holder exits, a waiting process that started during the window takes the lock, and that process can itself spawn further work. The lock ownership therefore moves between processes without any one of them being the root cause.
- **Orphaned processes resist cleanup by their spawner.** A process whose parent has exited is reparented to PID 1. The job that launched it can no longer reach it, so intervention must be manual.
- **A lock file is not a pre-flight check.** Adding a lock file to an index run protects the backup from overlapping itself, but it does not stop a process that already holds the database. The guard must check whether an index process is already running before starting.
- **Kill only at the timeout, and never with `-9`.** The sync hook's 3-hour timeout is the legitimate kill point; before that, a long-running process is treated as working rather than hung. Force-killing risks the index integrity the process was building.

## Details

The mechanism is ordinary for any file-backed store with an exclusive lock. What made this case hard to read is that the lock file existed and the holder was alive, so the usual reasoning, "the lock is stale, remove it," did not apply. The holder was the legitimate owner of the database; the failure was that a hook had started a second writer while the first was still legitimately using the store, and the first writer had outlived the context that was supposed to supervise it. A timeout that fires on the hook does not reach a process that has been reparented, which is why the 3-hour limit is the only effective bound in this configuration.

The debugging also corrected a tempting fix. Adding a lock file to every index run reads as a complete solution, but it only serializes runs that cooperate with the file. A process started before the lock convention existed, or one that holds the database without writing the file, bypasses the guard entirely. The durable control is a pre-flight check at the start of each run, asking whether a `memsearch index` process is already alive, combined with the lock file for the cases the check cannot see. The session scheduled both: lock-file checks on all index runs lacking them in the Friday 16 October harness slot, and a pre-flight check in the sync hook as a medium-term change.

The decision to wait rather than force-kill reflects the cost asymmetry of the operation. Killing a process mid-write can leave the index inconsistent, and the old `milvus.db.bak-*` directories were kept until the backup passed once, as a fallback if a rebuild proved necessary. The same session noted that the compiler-backlog hook failure for a missing 2026-10-09 log was still unresolved, which is a separate error in the same hook output and should not be conflated with the lock.

- [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]] — The accumulated causes of memsearch timeouts and failures, of which this lock chain is another.

# Connection: A Lock Whose Holder Outlived Its Purpose

## The Connection

The Milvus Lite lock contention of 2026-10-11 and the dead-PID lock of 2026-09-11 both describe a lock that outlives the work it was meant to guard, but they fail in opposite directions. In September the lock named a process that was already dead, so the retry was blocked by a claim that no longer had an owner. In October the lock was valid and its holder was alive, yet the holder had been reparented and no longer had a supervisor. The system could not reclaim the lock because it had no way to tell an active holder from an orphaned one.

## Key Insight

A lock file encodes a claim about the present. Checking whether the claim exists tells you that someone asserted ownership; it does not tell you that the owner is still doing work the system wants. The September case was resolved by testing whether the named PID was alive. The October case shows that this test is necessary but not sufficient: a live PID can be an orphan whose parent has exited, and such a process still holds the database while nothing above it can end it. The reliable question is whether the holder is still under a supervisor that will enforce a bound, and the answer is visible in the process tree, not in the lock file.

This is why the 3-hour timeout in the sync hook was the only effective kill point. A timeout belongs to the process that set it, and a reparented process has lost that parent. Designing a bound therefore means attaching it to something that will outlive the spawner, or checking for orphans explicitly at the start of each run. The pre-flight check adopted for the Milvus index is the second form: a new run asks whether an index process is already alive before it tries to take the lock, which turns a silent contention into an explicit decision.

## Evidence

- 2026-09-11: an OOM-killed backup left a memsearch lock naming a dead PID, with a second lock orphaned since August 5. Clearing the lock was safe because the holder was gone.
- 2026-10-11: process 64563 held the Milvus Lite lock with its parent exited and reparented to PID 1. The lock was valid, the holder was alive, and it could only be ended manually or by the 3-hour timeout. Adding a lock file to new runs was judged insufficient for this reason.
- 2026-10-11: the lock passed from process 14423 to 64563 in a cascade, so the lock's owner changed without any single process being the root cause.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/a-killed-process-leaves-debris-that-blocks-the-retry]] — The September case, where the holder was dead and the lock was pure debris.
- [[concepts/in-session-background-process-limits]] — Why a process started from a session can outlive the supervision that the session provides.

# Verification Round Reclassification Requires Secondary Review

A multi-agent verification workflow over 82 questions (Q01–Q82), run across 10 agent groups on 2026-10-11, produced 74 completed verifications before the session paused. Two questions changed classification during verification, and four were marked DEGRADED. The session's standing rule was that classification changes need a human review before merge, and that DEGRADED items need higher scrutiny than clean passes. The question set appears to be the same research-library pipeline described in related articles, though the log does not name it.

## Key Points

- **Classification flips are a review trigger, not a result.** Q23 changed EXCLUDE to INCLUDE and Q39 changed EXCLUDE to INCLUDE. Both were flagged for secondary review before the merge.
- **DEGRADED is a distinct status from failed.** Q47, Q48, Q70, and Q81 were marked DEGRADED. Q70 required eight corrections, so a DEGRADED item still carries usable output but needs closer reading than a clean pass.
- **A blocked group leaves a gap, not a failure of the rest.** The classifier blocked Q75–Q82 at launch; the other nine groups completed on schedule. The gap was reported explicitly rather than filled silently.
- **Two paths were offered for the gap.** Manually verify the eight questions, which was recommended since it avoided a new launch, or approve a fresh Opus launch, which is faster but risks another block. The decision was left to the user.

## Details

The verification round had the same shape as the batch work recorded elsewhere in this knowledge base: a set of items judged in parallel, a verdict per item, and a final merge. The new observation is in how the round handled its own outputs. A verification pass can change a prior classification, and a flip from EXCLUDE to INCLUDE alters what enters the final set, so the flip is itself a claim that needs its own check. The session treated the two flips as items for human review rather than as accepted corrections, which is the same discipline as keeping a terminal adjudicator in a review chain: the party that made the change does not also ratify it.

The DEGRADED tier is a useful intermediate status. A binary pass or fail would have either discarded Q70's useful content or accepted it with its eight corrections hidden. Keeping DEGRADED as its own state lets the merge proceed on the clean items while routing the degraded ones to closer reading, and it records how much correction each item needed. That matches the principle that a verification artifact should carry its own confidence, rather than presenting every output with the same authority.

The launch block is a reminder that parallel automation has coverage gaps that are not visible in the aggregate. Ten groups finishing on time looked like a complete round until the count showed 74 of 82. The session recorded the missing eight as an explicit open item with both remedies named, so the gap could not be mistaken for finished work at merge time.

# Memsearch: Setup, Python Migration Recovery, and Indexing

Memsearch is a local semantic search tool that indexes Claude Code's Tier A project-memory files, enabling cross-project retrieval of durable knowledge without directly accessing each project's files. On 2026-06-11, memsearch indexing failures were diagnosed and resolved: the root cause was a Python migration that left a hardcoded stale path inside memsearch.exe, making it unable to locate its runtime. Recovery required reinstalling memsearch into the new Python environment, re-applying the flush patch, and replacing the stale shim. After recovery, 805 chunks were confirmed indexed and searchable. On 2026-06-13, a concurrent-contention ETIMEDOUT pattern was observed and characterized. On 2026-06-17, the same Python-path-capture failure class was confirmed in a second tool. On 2026-07-27, a recurring indexing alarm was correctly re-diagnosed as structural — a first-time embedding index is an hours-scale job — and the reindex was relocated from the session-end hook to a nightly scheduled task. On 2026-09-30, a further run of timeouts was traced to a stopped dependency rather than to memsearch itself. On 2026-10-11, a macOS-side index run that had been going for 6 hours 41 minutes was stopped with SIGTERM, and a lock-holding orphan process was found to be blocking hook runs.

## Key Points

- **Cross-project Tier A search:** Tier A project-memory files (see [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]]) are cross-project searchable via memsearch — not siloed to a single project context.
- **Python migration breaks memsearch:** memsearch.exe embeds a path to the Python executable at install time. When Python is migrated — old installation deleted, new one installed at a different path — memsearch fails because its embedded path is no longer valid. The failure is an install-time path capture becoming stale, not a configuration issue.
- **Recovery sequence (three steps):** reinstall memsearch into the new Python environment; re-apply the flush patch (the modification enabling Stop-hook integration); replace the stale shim file with one pointing to the new installation. After recovery on 2026-06-11, 805 chunks were indexed and confirmed searchable.
- **`index` command requires explicit paths:** memsearch's `index` command does not auto-discover project memory directories; the hook or invocation script must pass explicit file and directory paths, which makes indexing scope deterministic and auditable.
- **Timeouts and stalls have at least four distinct causes.** (1) *Concurrent contention* — multiple sessions or background jobs writing the same index produce non-fatal ETIMEDOUTs (6 in 24 hours on 2026-06-13); the index is not corrupted and later invocations succeed. (2) *Structural overrun* — a first-time embedding index is hours-scale and cannot fit a 45-second hook. (3) *A stopped dependency* — the late-September timeouts traced to Docker's Milvus container being down, not to broken memsearch code. (4) *Single-writer lock held by an orphan* — on macOS, Milvus Lite allows one writer, and a reparented index process can hold the lock for hours; see [[concepts/milvus-lite-single-writer-lock-contention]].
- **Stopping a long index run leaves the index in an unknown state.** On 2026-10-11 a 6 h 41 min run (PID 59218) was stopped with SIGTERM and exited cleanly. The index may be partial afterward, so its state must be checked before deciding whether to rerun.
- **Silent `exit 1` (2026-06-13):** a separate failure class from ETIMEDOUTs, with no surviving diagnostic output and an unknown cause; if recurring, it warrants adding stderr capture to the hook script.
- **Python path-capture staleness affects standard venvs too (2026-06-17):** the `morning-briefing` pipeline's `.venv` was broken from 2026-06-12 because its `pyvenv.cfg` referenced a removed `C:\Python314`. The fix is identical in structure: rebuild against the current Python.
- **Reindex relocated to a nightly scheduled task (2026-07-27):** the heavy reindex moved into the 6:15 AM `daily-backup.ps1` task — uncapped, using the full `memsearch.exe` path, escalating per-path failures, resetting the hook timeout-streak counter on success. The session-end hook stays a light 45-second incremental pass, with its alarm threshold raised 3→6 so it fires only when the nightly safety net itself falls behind.

## Details

The Python shebang path problem in memsearch represents a distinct class of tool-configuration staleness from environment-variable and PATH issues. Unlike `setx` propagation failures or Task Scheduler PATH omissions, the memsearch issue lives in the tool's own binary: a specific file path was captured at install time and embedded in the executable. When that path ceases to exist, the binary fails at startup regardless of what the current environment looks like. The diagnostic fingerprint is: `memsearch.exe` appears to exist, its location is on PATH, but running it produces errors about Python or interpreter paths. The correct remediation is reinstallation — not PATH configuration — because the problem is inside the binary. The flush patch must be re-applied after any reinstallation, since reinstalling produces a fresh unmodified binary; the durable practice is to document the patch, reinstall cleanly, then re-apply.

The accumulated timeout findings now form a short differential diagnosis, and the 2026-09-30 and 2026-10-11 results are the cautionary ones. In September, a recurring, code-shaped symptom had a root cause outside memsearch: a stopped Docker container hosting the Milvus vector store. In October, a long-running macOS index with a valid but orphaned lock was blocking later hook runs, and the operator's stop left the index in a state that had to be verified rather than assumed. The visible failure mode of memsearch, a timeout or a stall, is nearly uninformative about cause, so the diagnosis must start by checking the dependency chain — is the vector store up, is a first-time index still running, is another process holding the lock, is another session writing the same index — before any code is suspected. The 2026-09-30 session also confirmed that a neighboring failure in the same error log, a 2026-09-27 memory-flush failure, was a Claude usage-limit hit rather than a pipeline bug, reinforcing that a shared error log mixes resource events, quota events, and genuine defects under similar-looking lines.

The 2026-06-17 morning-briefing venv failure generalizes the Python path-capture staleness to a broader class. Both memsearch.exe (compiled binary with embedded interpreter path) and a standard `.venv` (whose `pyvenv.cfg` records `home = C:\Python314`) become non-functional when that Python is removed; the detection pattern and the fix are identical. The 2026-07-27 relocation of the heavy reindex into the nightly backup task resolved the structural case: with the hours-scale work on a nightly cadence that runs uncapped, the session-end hook is left as a light incremental pass and its consecutive-miss alarm becomes a real signal instead of chronic noise, while the full library index converges over a night or two and incremental search stays live throughout.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.
